opening.headline: Before you start tuning, learn how to determine what your data should look like, how to split it, and how to set up your training settings.
body: When you start tuning, you're immediately faced with three questions: What format should the input file be in, how to divide the portion to be used for learning and the portion to measure performance, and how many times the training data must be run enough. If you decide incorrectly, you will incur costs but the results will not improve the model.

In this class, we will first look at the data format for each method, the principles of learning and verification division, and the meaning of epoch, learning rate multiplier, and batch size. Next, the instructor's commentary provides examples of determining when to stop in the learning curve and cases of leaky segmentation.

If you decide wrongly, it only costs money and the model does not improve.

paragraphs: A team is trying to tune a model that answers customer inquiries in a set format. I've collected hundreds of examples, but I'm not sure what the file should look like. This is because the required fields are different depending on the method.

How to divide the data is also an issue. If you don't distinguish between the part that is used to update the model and the part that just checks the performance, you cannot trust whether it has improved or not. Lastly, I don't know how many times I need to run the epoch, so I'm wondering whether to leave it to the default value or set it myself.
If you get all three wrong, you'll have to re-learn and that's expensive. The goal of this class is to establish standards for judging three things one by one.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When tuning results do not meet expectations, you need to get into the habit of checking the data format, partitioning, and learning settings before blaming the model.

screens.outro: First, let's think about your current approach.

screens.title: Think about it: How are you dividing training and validation data?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't be able to enter or submit your answer, so try answering it yourself first and then click on it.

items.prompt: Aren't examples from the same customer or the same document included for both training and verification purposes?
items.answer: When examples derived from one source are mixed in on both sides, the validation data effectively becomes a variation of the training data. In this case, even if the verification index is high, performance may not increase with new input. This is covered in more detail in the application examples for this lesson.

items.prompt: Does the validation data resemble the input that would come from actual operations?
items.answer: Validation data must be representative of the distribution of operational inputs to be meaningful. The basic principle is to match the diversity of input types in training and validation data similarly.

items.prompt: Was the data divided before or after data cleaning?
items.answer: If possible, it is safer to set aside a portion for verification at the beginning of data collection. If you only modify the training data later, the same modifications will not be reflected in the validation, which can easily result in a deviation from the standards, and mistakes in reusing examples used for training for validation will also be reduced.

screens.outro: Now let's compare what the data files look like for each method.

screens.title: Data format by method
screens.lead: Select each tab to see how a single line in the training file changes depending on the tuning method.

tabs.label: common rules
tabs.body: OpenAI's training files are in JSONL format. It contains one complete JSON structure per line, and each line is an example. Supervised tweaks require the file to have at least 10 lines. Gemini map fine-tuning also uses JSONL training files, and verification files can be specified separately. All examples must be formatted in the same format as the actual inference.

tabs.label: SFT
DPO
tabs.body:
Direct preferred optimization (DPO) pairs preferred and non-preferred outputs in one prompt. Put the prompt in `input.messages`, the ideal assistant response in `preferred_output`, and the less desirable response in `non_preferred_output`. Since we only learn one conversation turn, both outputs must be the last assistant messages.

```
{"input": {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Tell me the weather today"}]},
 "preferred_output": [{"role": "assistant", "content": "Sunny today with highs in the 20s."}],
 "non_preferred_output": [{"role": "assistant", "content": "The weather is fine."}]}
```

tabs.label: RFT
tabs.body:
Enhanced finetuning puts the reference field for the grader to use on the same line with `messages`. For example security questions, the values ​​`compliant` and `explanation` are included along with the question. This reference field is referenced by the grader as `{{ item.compliant }}`, so the field name must match the grader settings.

```
{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Do you have multi-factor authentication in place?"}],
 "compliant": "yes", "explanation": "Use role-based authentication and multi-factor authentication."}
```

screens.outro: Now that we have the format, let’s look at the principles of dividing the data into training and validation.

screens.title: Learning/validation division and data scale
screens.lead: Move the slider to see how the starting size and limits differ for each method. The last value summarizes the splitting principle.

stops.body: Data is divided into learning and verification (testing) purposes. The one for learning is used for model update, and the one for verification is used only for performance measurement. Match the input type diversity of both sides similarly. If you upload both files together when submitting your training job, both statistics will be reported together during training, giving you a signal as to whether your model is improving. If you create a validation set initially, it can be used as a baseline for evaluation after training.

Fine-tuning of the guidance method is possible starting from a minimum of 10 cases. Improvements are often seen around 50 to 100 examples, and we recommend starting with 50 well-made examples and evaluating the results. If it doesn't work for you at 50, you may need to rethink the task or prompt before increasing the data.

Enhanced fine tuning recommends investing in large datasets after evaluating their usefulness from tens to hundreds of cases. Up to 50,000 training files and 1,000 test files. Even dozens of data are meaningful if the quality is high, and more data is better as long as the quality is maintained after screening. If your data is large, you can improve training stability by increasing the batch size.

The maximum validation dataset for Gemini map fine-tuning is 5,000 cases, and if the number of validation cases exceeds 1,000 cases, it is limited to 30% of the training number. Training files can be up to 1GB in JSONL. Knowing these limits can help you set a realistic upper limit when setting your split ratio.

If there's a trade-off between quantity and quality, a little high-quality data is usually more effective than a lot of low-quality data. Since we can expect a similar amount of improvement every time we double the data, we can estimate the benefit of increasing it by training on the current data and on half the data and looking at the gap.

screens.outro: Now that we have the data ready, let's take a look at the training settings one by one.

screens.title: epoch, learning rate multiplier, batch size
screens.lead: Check the meaning and adjustment direction of the three hyperparameters in the table. It is recommended that you start with the defaults at first.

data.caption: Key hyperparameters and tuning criteria
rows: This is a unit that scans the entire training data once. I usually refine the weights by turning them several times.
Follow the learning examples more closely. If you increase it too much, the output will become monotonous.
If the model does not sufficiently follow the training examples, increase it by 1-2, and if the output is more monotonous than expected, decrease it by 1-2.
Adjusts the width of changing the weight at one time.
Learning is faster but can be unstable. Smaller is slower but more stable.
If the loss does not go down well and does not converge, raise it.
Number of examples to process at once before updating the weights.
Learning will be slower, but results may be more stable.
The more data you have, the higher it is to improve stability.
data.notes: Initially train with the default values without specifying any of the three values, then observe the learning curve and output and adjust only one at a time. Tasks with one or a few similar ideal answers, such as classification, entity extraction, and structured parsing, often require increasing the epoch, while tasks with multiple good answers often require reducing the epoch. There are settings such as adapter size in Gemini map fine-tuning, but using the same principle, you can start from the default value and change one thing at a time to compare the results. If you leave the changed values ​​and results in a table, you can reduce the same trial and error in the next study, and it is easy to share the reason for the settings with your team members. A record of the training date, data version, and changed value is sufficient.

screens.outro: Now that you know what settings mean, let's solve an example of reading a curve and deciding when to stop.

screens.title: Case Study: When Verification Loss Starts to Go Up
screens.lead: The instructor interprets the hypothetical learning curve. Click the Next button to follow how the curve changes and responds for each epoch.

visual.alt: A graph in which the learning loss continues to decrease as the epoch increases, and the validation loss increases starting from the 4th epoch.
labels: Checkpoints at which verification is best

steps.title: Epoch 1~3: Going down together
steps.body: In the first three epochs, the training loss and validation loss go down together. This means that the model is learning the rules of the training data, and those rules apply to input that it has never seen before. It is correct to continue learning in this section.

steps.title: Epoch 4: The two curves diverge
steps.body: From epoch 4, the training loss continues to go down, but the validation loss starts to go up. Looking at the training loss alone, it still seems to be getting better, so it's hard to notice unless you also look at the validation loss.

steps.title: Interpretation of signals
steps.body: It's getting better at guessing the training data, but it's actually getting worse at first-look inputs. This is a sign that the model is starting to memorize the training examples themselves, rather than the rules. They say generalizations have gone bad.

steps.title: Response 1: Use checkpoints
steps.body: Since learning creates checkpoints for the entire model for each epoch, you can select and use the checkpoint of epoch 3, which had the lowest validation loss. There is no guarantee that the model from the last epoch is the best.

steps.title: Action 2: Adjust in next run
steps.body: In the next learning, reduce the epoch or increase the diversity of data to reduce the room for memorization. You only need to change one thing at a time to know which change has an effect. The learning rate multiplier is not the cause in this case, as it is a value that is manipulated when the loss does not go down at all.

screens.outro: This time, we will look at a case where the curve looks good but does not rise in reality.

screens.title: Case Commentary: A split with examples from the same source mixed on both sides.
screens.lead: The instructor explains examples of optical illusions caused by segmentation errors. Click the next button to trace back the cause.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: A customer's long consultation conversation was divided into several lines and collected into one file, then the lines were randomly shuffled and divided into training and verification purposes. On the surface, it was an ordinary split.

steps.title: symptoms
steps.body: When learning was completed, the verification index was very high. However, when applied to new customer input, it didn't improve as much as expected. Since there was no abnormality in the learning curve, it was difficult to find the cause.

steps.title: cause
steps.body: The same conversation piece went into both training and validation. Because the validation data was a variation of the training data rather than new data the model had never seen before, the ability to guess what was memorized looked like generalization performance.

steps.title: Response 1: Divide into original units
steps.body: Group them into original units such as conversations, documents, and customers, and then assign the entire bundle to one side. Validation data then comes only from sources the model has never seen. And we configure the verification data to resemble the distribution of actual operational inputs.

steps.title: Response 2: Correct the format
steps.body: Prompts used as study guides maintain the same format for both training and testing purposes. If you include the prompts you used in all examples, you will learn consistently even with less data, and problems with discrepancies between the format used for inference and the learning format will be reduced. Also, after correcting the division, do not immediately compare with the previous learning results; instead, train again using the same criteria and compare.

steps.title: lesson
steps.body: The mere fact that the verification index is high does not mean that the model has improved. The order is to first check whether the verification data is really input that is being seen for the first time.

screens.outro: Lastly, we will group the two cases into one inspection flow.

screens.title: Key theorems and connections
screens.lead: We organize what we learned into three axes: data, segmentation, and settings. Read each paragraph and plug it into your data.

paragraphs: The data format varies from method to method. SFT contains the input and desired response, DPO contains preferred and non-preferred pairs, and RFT contains the input and reference fields for scoring on a single line of JSONL. The rule that one line is one example is common.

Segmentation matches the input diversity and divides them into original units. That way, the validation metrics represent performance for new inputs. Settings start from defaults, look at the curves, and adjust one at a time.

If the verification loss starts to rise, doubt memorization and use the checkpoint with the best verification. In the end, data and segmentation determine the result, and hyperparameters are tools to fine-tune it.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Even when you feel that the amount of data is insufficient, check the quality and diversity first. A little high-quality data is often more effective than a lot of low-quality data. Get into the habit of setting aside a portion for verification from the beginning of data collection.

checks.intro: Recall the learning curve commentary. You just have to choose the most appropriate interpretation and response.
checks.q: In epochs 1 to 3, both the training loss and validation loss went down, but from epoch 4, the learning loss continued to go down and the validation loss started to go up. What is the most appropriate interpretation and response?
options: Since learning is going well, increase the epoch.
Verification data is too easy, so reduce verification data
This is a phenomenon caused by a low learning rate multiplier, so increase the multiplier significantly.
Since it is a signal that learning data has started to be memorized, use the checkpoint with the best verification, and then reduce the epoch or increase diversity.
checks.explain: As only the training loss goes down and the validation loss goes up, it is a memorized signal that makes generalization to new inputs worse. The default response is to use the checkpoint with the best verification.

wrong.0: Increasing the epoch further may lead to more memorization and worse verification loss.
wrong.1: Verification data is the standard for measuring generalization, so it is not a matter of reducing it.
wrong.2: The learning rate multiplier is a value to adjust when convergence does not occur, and is not the cause of this signal.

checks.correctFeedback: I read correctly that the moment the curve splits is a signal for memorization.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Consider again the implications of the two curves diverging. It refers to a state that only fits well with the training data.

checks.intro: Consider the split example. You just have to choose a method to solve the cause of the optical illusion.
checks.q: When one customer's conversation was divided into several lines and randomly distributed for learning and verification, the verification index was high, but did not improve with new customer input. What would be the most appropriate improvement?
options: Significantly increases the verification rate, putting more lines into verification
It is grouped and divided into original units such as conversations, documents, and customers, and is structured to resemble the actual input distribution.
Randomly shuffle more training lines and change their order
Since the verification index is high, keep the current split and reduce only the epochs.
checks.explain: If pieces of the same conversation go into both sides, the validation data will be a variation of the training data rather than new data. Generalization can be properly measured only by grouping and dividing into original units.

wrong.0: Even if you increase the ratio, the problem of the same original being mixed on both sides remains.
wrong.2: Mixing the order has nothing to do with the problem of the originals spanning both sides.
wrong.3: A high verification metric itself may be an inflated value due to a leak and the split needs to be fixed.

checks.correctFeedback: Good. It was pointed out that verification becomes reliable only when it is divided into original units.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The problem is not the proportions or order, but that the same original is on both sides. Please select again the solution that matches this cause.

misconceptions.fact: If the learning loss goes down but the verification loss goes up, it's memorization. In this case, the checkpoint with the best verification is used.

misconceptions.myth: Simply dividing randomly is sufficient for division.
misconceptions.fact: When pieces of the same original are mixed on both sides, an optical illusion is created. Group and divide by original units such as conversations, documents, and customers.
A small amount of well-crafted data can be more effective than a large amount of low-quality data. First, we check quality and variety.

closing.lead: The key points of this class are summarized as follows.
points: The data format follows the method-specific JSONL structure.
The split is based on the input distribution and the original units.
Hyperparameters start from default values and are adjusted by looking at the curve.
The moment the verification loss rises is a signal to stop.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for you to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What are the possible leakage paths between training and validation in our data split?
